content: An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is defined as a localized enlargement of the abdominal aorta that exceeds the normal diameter of the vessel by more than 50%. On average, the normal diameter of the infrarenal aorta is approximately 2 cm.0 cm or greater. Aortic ectasia, on the other hand, refers to a mild, generalized dilation of the aorta that is less than 50% of the normal diameter, typically measuring ≤2.9 cm. This condition is often attributed to age-related degenerative changes in the vessel walls. Abdominal aortic aneurysms are considered life-threatening conditions that require immediate medical attention, regardless of the underlying cause. Some of the life-threatening causes of AAA include abdominal trauma, bacteremia, gastrointestinal perforation, and vertebral osteomyelitis. Common causes of abdominal aortic aneurysms include abdominal trauma, atherosclerosis, and genetic conditions such as Marfan syndrome. A Focused Initial Rapid Evaluation (FIRE) is a critical step in the management of patients suspected of having an abdominal aortic aneurysm. This evaluation is designed to quickly identify individuals who require urgent intervention. Following the FIRE process, a complete diagnostic approach should be undertaken to confirm the diagnosis and guide further management. This comprehensive diagnostic workup is performed after any necessary emergency interventions have been initiated. The treatment of abdominal aortic aneurysms is guided by established clinical algorithms and guidelines. These protocols outline the appropriate steps for managing the condition, including surgical and non-surgical options, depending on the size of the aneurysm, the presence of symptoms, and the patient’s overall health status.
